utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer, Lisa Biersay, Thomas Laugel, and Ivana Martinovic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stoparic. Let me remind you that you are still under oath. Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yesterday we ended when you were discussing the building where you went to to register as a volunteer with the TO of the SBWS. And this morning, I'd like to pick up on that. And specifically I'd like you to describe to the Trial Chamber the people that you saw and recognised on the day that you went to register.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the man who I believe was the main person in that office who in the end gave me some sort of certificate was called Filipovic. There were other people there. There were some women in uniform who were making coffee. But that man, Filipovic, I believe, was person number one because when I came I produced my ID, and he said, I don't need your ID. You have to give me your military service book. I didn't have it on me, so I went back home and brought back my military service book because he said the JNA does not allow people who have war-time assignment in their military service book to register. I did not have a war-time assignment, so I was able to register. Then I went to the other building, which was the seat of the peacetime TO. That's where I got a uniform and I got a weapon in an area of Sid called Vasariste.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could just step back for one moment. Do you recall what Mr. Filipovic was wearing at the time you were in the recruitment office?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time, when I saw him later, including on TV, he was wearing a red jacket. That's how I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described him as the main person. Did you recognise any other individuals associated with the government of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew all those people. They are from the area. I didn't know this Filipovic, but I knew other people. Some were from Tovarnik or the environs. From the locality. The man who was linked to the government, among others, was a man called Grahovac. I saw him several times too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, turning to tab 18, please, which is 65 ter number 443. And it's dated 18 October 1991. And this document was previously discussed with the witness just before Mr. Stoparic. I'd like to direct your attention to the upper right-hand corner where it lists the place and the date. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It -- it's probably that certificate or a document made in Sid on 18th of October, 1991, Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at the bottom, there is a -- it says "for the chief" and the signature Dusan Filipovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the middle of that document, it reads: "The remaining part of the unit is registered with the commander of the unit. "Commander Milan Lancuzanin is responsible for the activities of the unit." And it's referring to the Leva Supoderica detachment. Do you recognise the name Milan Lancuzanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my commander. That was my commander at the time. Milan Lancuzanin, also mean as Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 443 please. 65 ter number 443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't know how the Registrar does this, but he tells me that this is a document part of the Theunens package.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Exactly. And I did mention that it was used with him. As we did with Mr. Theunens where documents that were specifically discussed individually were moved for admission, this separate, and I think because the witness is able to speak about it, it can be admitted separately from the package. Once the package is prepared for consideration, we'll already have a P number for it and it won't be before the Court for consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1727. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that you received your weapon from the peacetime -- excuse me, your uniform from the peacetime TO. Is that correct? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what I said, but I meant that in that building of the local commune of Sid there were offices even before the war of the Territorial Defence, and from their depots we got uniforms, the old uniforms, the old type. We called them SNB. That means olive-green-grey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which TO are we talking about now when you say there are offices even before the war of the Territorial Defence? Do you mean the SBWS or another TO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's most probably the Yugoslav TO or the TO of the Republic of Serbia. I don't know how it was divided then. In my mind, it was the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you went to receive your weapon, what forces were present?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army. There was a non-commissioned officer who distributed weapons to us from a case on top of a truck. It was conserved weapons in their lubricant. We had to clean them first. And there by the depots a unit was formed that was headed by Zeljko Krnjajic. He had a deputy named Vojkapic. I was one of the men who received weapons there who tried the weapons to test them to see if they work correctly. So it was the Yugoslav People's Army that provided us with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now you describe in your statement that you later went to Tovarnik. Could you describe the -- the convoy that went from Sid to Tovarnik with volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go to Tovarnik in a convoy of vehicles. Instead, coming halfway, we got off the Pinzgauers and we deployed in a line: One vehicle, a man, then one vehicle, one man. And then getting closer to Tovarnik we got hand-grenades, and the shooting already started there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say coming halfway, what do you mean? Coming halfway of what? From the journey from Sid to Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Sid and Tovarnik are very close to one another. From the centre of the village, I can see the square in Tovarnik. It's about 5 or 6 kilometres, so somewhere halfway is the border between Serbia and the territory of Tovarnik, which is Croatia. So we were standing right there at the border, and that's where we fanned out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you say that from Sid you could see the square in Tovarnik. Where there any landmarks that you could specifically see from Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that to describe how close it was. You could see the tower of the church. Every village has a church and the type of church depends of the ethnic community which is in the majority there. That's what I meant to say, that we were very close.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you went from Sid to Tovarnik, did you have your weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my automatic rifle, I had a knife that comes with it, I had a combat set of ammunition, and I believe a gas mask as well. And the hand-grenades we received when we were already close to the village of Tovarnik, just before the shooting started. There was a NCO from the Royal Motorised Brigade who distributed hand-grenades to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, when you say "NCO," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said officer, and NCO is a non-commissioned officer up to the rank of warrant officer. Second-lieutenant and lieutenant are already officers. I meant the person who works in the army is -- with a mid-level education is an NCO. Those with a high education, with degrees, they are officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you participated in the takeover of Tovarnik in September of 1991, who are the company commanders of the Territorial Defence of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the one to which I belonged. That was Zeljko Krnjajic. I don't know about the others. I don't know who commanded what unit. In that area, even locals of Serb ethnicity joined. The first day they received weapons or they already had weapons. So it's all a bit of a blur. I know about my unit. The commander was Krnjajic and his deputy was Vojkapic. My platoon commander was somebody from Novi Sad. I know his name only, Sasa.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: From who did you and others in your unit receive orders while you were in Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Krnjajic. He issued orders. Or Vojkapic, his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, in paragraph 12 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, for reference, it is 65 ter number 5977.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- you -- and we don't need to look at it, but you describe seeing many dead bodies of Croatian civilians in the streets of Tovarnik. And my question is: How did you know that those people were Croatians?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also saw a Serb woman. I knew it was a Serb woman because she was the grandmother of a friend of mine in Sid. I knew because that village -- I mean, when I say "I knew," I assumed because that village was -- I don't know the exact percentage, but equally populated in an equal ratio between Serbs and Croats, and I suppose that if those bodies were Serb, then their families would have removed the bodies already, taken them away. Since they were lying there, I thought they were Croats. And there were two or three in uniform among them. Uniforms of the Croatian army or police, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were most of these bodies that you saw?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have never been in a war, so you don't know, but we went through yards. I saw some bodies in the yards of houses, and the next day I saw several bodies near the petrol station, and the military police was guarding them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know when or how these civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But during the first day of combat operations, there were no bodies there. We passed by the petrol station, but when we went back the next day, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what information, if any, did you have about what had happened to those people whose body you saw?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somebody killed them, executed them, or whatever. Maybe the soldiers had taken them out of their own gardens and yards, but I don't believe so. They would have put them on a truck if they had removed then. They were just lying there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to move from Tovarnik to Vukovar. Mr. Stoparic, how long before the fall of Vukovar did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in September from the Lipovaca camp and stayed there until the end. I don't know how long that was. I received two months' salaries for that period. Now, how long exactly I spent there, I don't know. They might have overpaid me, like, by five or six days. Anyway, it counted as two months' salary. I had a certificate that I received at Velepromet that I was a member of Leva Supoderica, stating the period when I was at Vukovar. However, a warrant officer took that certificate from me when he was paying out my salary, so I don't know exactly how many days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you paid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at Topcider. It's the barracks of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, could you list the -- for the Trial Chamber the forces that were present in Vukovar when you were there, the ones that you knew of.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those that I knew about. We were there, the unit of Leva Supoderica. There was the Guards Brigade. In our sector, there was also the Territorial Defence. I will say TO for short. Don't ask me to say every time Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. There was the TO. There were two commanders there. One was Stanko Vujanovic, one was Miroljub. I forget his last name now, but I'll remember it later. That was on our side where I was involved in combat operations. On the other side, there was the Arkan's units and probably the Novi Sad corps. I don't know about any others. There were probably reservists there too. Maybe there were more volunteer groups but I don't know their names and I didn't run into them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "on our side, and then you say "on the other side," what do you mean by "our side?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Vukovar from the direction of Negoslavci. Petrova Gora. There were other axes, such as Sotin. I believe the operations in Vukovar were divided into south and north. I was on the south side, and I believe those groups in the north were working on the other side of the city. We from Leva Supoderica did Sveto Naselje, Petrovo Brdo, and such.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we now please have tab 8, which is 65 ter number 6317, on the screen, please. And this should be a Google map of the Vukovar area that was generated last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what I'll ask you to do, Mr. Stoparic, is to identify some locations of the relevant forces that you just described.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't have to be 100 per cent correct. It's going to be roughly about my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Right. But one minute. But one minute, Mr. Stoparic. I just wanted to ... Can you -- can you see clearly those areas that you are familiar with? Just in general.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. So, for example, you describe the south and the north. Could you perhaps draw the dividing line of those two sections?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll draw a dividing line showing the part of the city where I did not go. I believe it's something like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And which side were you on for the -- the south?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mark where our headquarters was and where we spent the nights when we were not in action. This is Nova Ulica, Nova street, so it's somewhere here, and we slept in these houses around. Two houses here were used as a headquarters. One was a small depot and one was the headquarters of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now if could you draw a circle around those dots that you've made and draw a line to the side and just put number 1 so that later we can follow what the markings are.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the houses. And you described Vujanovic as being a commander. Where was he located primarily?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly where he was based. I don't know. But I know where his men were deployed. I can show you that. I know where they held the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where is that, if you could please mark it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the 1st of May Street, then they held the line from here to here. Or maybe even up to here. So this sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you mark that with a number 2. I see that you've circled it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is Leva Supoderica also a neighbourhood of the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were two neighbourhoods. One was called Leva Supoderica, another was Desna Supoderica. Other neighbourhoods were Petro Gora, Mitnica, and others, and I think it's to the left from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber -- well, first let me ask you: Did you have a chance to see the Petrova Gora neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I came to this street. I mean, I went by way of Petrova Gora. Actually, all of this is Petrova Gora, I think. The houses, they were well-preserved. They were not completely destroyed. Anyway, they were inhabitable. They didn't leak. I think that all of this was Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know what the predominant ethnicity was of the Petrova Gora neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain because the whole city was mixed. But I think that by chance it was the Serbs who were the majority in Petrova Gora. But don't take my word for it. There were both Croats and Serbs in the town, but there were also Slovaks and Hungarians and so on. I do believe, though, that the Serbs had the largest share in Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you know on this map where the SBWS TO forces were located?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on where activities were launched, they were always next to us. We were doing things, they were doing things. Not sure what you mean. I showed you where the front line was at some point. Of course, it moved. But what I described was the situation during the first week. This is the 1st of May Street here, and that's where the front line was. Although I can't see the name of the street here, but this should be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber the structure of combat deployment for actions.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organisation was as in any other army. There were companies, platoons, squads, and the army would present us their plan. It was usually Captain Zirojevic [phoen] who came to us, or Captain Radic. They would bring aerial maps and then the table of code-names to use, and then they would say where they would -- artillery preparation, where we would go in. We would usually be in the middle, and Miroljub and Stanko would be on the left and right sides respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "we," do you mean the Leva Supoderica detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the command of Kameni. I mean the Leva Supoderica detachment. Because, as far as I know, officially we were volunteers of the Guards Brigade. The TO was separate. Of course, they also had links with the JNA. But most of us at Leva Supoderica were from outside, from Serbia. Although there were locals too. The commander was a local. And there were also other people from the area, the town and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Regarding Captain Radic, could you describe with what unit or brigade he was with.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer of the Guards Brigade. I'm not sure now whether it was the 1st Guards Brigade or whatever the exact name was. I'll simply stick to Guards Brigade. At the time he was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, in your statement, you describe Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic, and I notice that sometimes when you're speaking you refer simply to Stanko and Miroljub, am I correct that when you use those first names, you're referring to those two people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And this is not for you, Mr. Stoparic. I'm trying to fill in the transcript. So you describe in your statement Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic. That's just for the record. When you had these meetings, were Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic always there on time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanko would mostly come on time, but Miroljub always came late and sometimes didn't come at all. Stanko came more often. Where the headquarters was, I believe that one of the houses close was his own private house. He came often. But when -- whenever there was a meeting, when we would -- we would try to agree how we would go about things, where we would attack, he would always come late. He had his own headquarters because, you know, the TO is actually not the main player in war. It's the JNA. And the TO also had responsibilities toward the district and who knows what they had to do. But that's probably how things were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to direct your attention to the day you were serving as a duty officer at the command post of Leva Supoderica. Do you recall that morning?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, or, rather, that evening, Ovcara happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And while you were at the command post, do you recall receiving some urgent phone calls in the morning?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, our commander and many officers, that is, all company commanders, had left for Belgrade. They weren't there. They weren't in Vukovar as all. They went to see Seselj at the Radical Party. And Miroljub called and asked for Kameni a number of times. Then we gave him the phone number of the place where Kameni was and probably he called him there. He didn't call us any longer. Because we had this military-style telephone at our headquarters and Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, we still have that marked map on the screen. Is that okay with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For now, yes, Your Honour. I will go ahead and tender it now and we can come back to it if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you see Kameni that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, when he got there. Before that, I spoke to him on the spoken. Because I was a duty officer day and night and he had taken everybody else with him, so there was no one to relieve me. I tried a number of times to contact him but he was not available. And he told me, Well, do stay on for a little longer and then there will be someone to relieve you. And then Kinez came, Mare, Djo, Ceca, these are the nicknames of our officers. I will give you their true names later. I may have forgotten some names but I remember most of them. Later he asked for the count of men, and then I went to see the platoon commanders or squad commanders to inquire, and then I gave him the information. And Kameni said, I'm not interested in those who are absent with leave because some did have leave to go and see their families. He was interested in those who had gone AWOL.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you said those names very quickly when you were discussing people who were with Kameni. Could you repeat them again, please, and say them a little bit more slowly so that we can record them on the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Kameni, that's Milan Lancuzanin, the commander. He was accompanied by the commander of the 1st Company, Kinez. His true name is Predrag Milojevic. The 2nd Company commander, I forget his name but we called him Ceca. And there was another commander whose true name I also forget but we called him Mare, and one more commander who we called Mali Djo, little Joe. I may remember some names later, but we usually call each other by nicknames so that's why I remember those better.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What does the nickname Kinez mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kinez, it means the Chinese in English, or Chinaman. He had almond eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now direct your attention, and I'd like you to actually see it so you know what I mean. This is tab 1, your statement, 65 ter number 5977. And in the English, it would be on page 8, paragraph 36. Now in 36 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: There's a sentence that reads: "They returned around noon." Do you see that sentence? And you're talking about Kameni, Ceca, Kinez, and Djo. And when you say they returned around noon, where did they return to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably to Vukovar because he called me. He couldn't have called me from Belgrade using a Motorola. Or, actually, that's wrong. I called him a number of times, and then once he actually answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And then -- so if I understand you correctly, they returned around noon to the Vukovar area, and that's where you believe they contacted you by Motorola?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all. Only the commander, Kameni. I saw them on that evening, when they all came to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how -- how is it that, in your mind, you're giving the time of when they came to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was November. Around 5.00 it -- it gets dark. Maybe even earlier. But I'm not sure I really understand your question. You mean based on what I know that they actually -- actually came in the evening? Well, because it was evening. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you remember --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lights were on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You remember the time, is that --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I remember, yes. I don't know what else to say. That's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, when you first began answering the question, you said it was the day of -- or the day of the Ovcara killing. How soon did you learn about the Ovcara killings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know back then or at that moment. But I asked Kameni, What's happening? Why do you need the numbers of those present? And then he said, Things are happening that shouldn't be happening. And a few hours later, the first rumours arrived about large-scale executions. I didn't know it was about Ovcara though. Only on the following day I learned that the site of the killings was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'd now like to fast forward --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, excuse me, a soldier of mine also told me - a platoon commander - he said that he had been at Ovcara and that he had killed people with his knife. I didn't believe him, of course. But now he is convicted. He got 20 years' of imprisonment in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djordje, Soskic. He was in my platoon. I was his platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Stoparic, in either 2002 or 2003 when you had a meeting with Kameni, Ceca, and Kinez?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really socialise with Kameni, but we met every day. We lived in the same town. He had a number of cerebral strokes though and he was an invalid, and he would always call me or a relative of his when he to go somewhere because he was afraid of going by car on his own. So I was there to help him with his private affairs, and once rumours started spreading that the Ovcara incident would be taken to court in Serbia, they started meeting to decide what to say when the police started interviewing them. Kinez was even interviewed and connected to a polygraph. I think, though, that most of what they said was actually true. Of course, I don't really know what happened at Ovcara because I didn't see any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did Kameni have a point of view about what was to be said about the time that he arrived at the command post where you were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how he phrased it, but they must have arrived at the command post earlier and that they had been at Ovcara and seen what was happening, that Kameni tried to save a neighbour but Miroljub didn't let him. And Kameni told his people, Let's get out of here. And that was the story. And I can neither corroborate nor deny it because I wasn't there. But I told you when he came to the headquarters, it was evening-time. And during the day, we spoke to each other, that's true. But what really happened there, I can only suppose and stick to the Belgrade judgements. They were all convicted, all but one who was acquitted. Everybody else was convicted. Mare was acquitted, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If I could have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, I'd like to play a clip. It's found at tab 95, and it's 65 ter number 4885.1. And I will be playing this without the sound. And after watching parts of this clip, then I'll show some stills and ask Mr. Stoparic if he recognises the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stoparic, we'll just let this -- this run and then I'll ask you about it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Pause it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry -- sorry. I don't why this clip is without sound. It has the sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It does have a sound. I'm not asking Mr. Stoparic to opine on the contents. It's merely for identification of the people. And if the -- I believe the interpreters do have the transcript that we delivered, but I'm not asking Mr. Stoparic about the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to talk about the very last image that we saw in this clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, for the record, this clip goes from 02 hours, 49 minutes, 21 second, to 02 hours, 49 minutes, 37 seconds; and then to 02 hour, 52 minute, and 25 seconds to 02 hour and 59 minutes and 37 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just re-playing it because what I'd like to do is freeze at the very end and ask if you recognise anyone. I know you recognised some people in this part, but we don't talk about this right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, do you recognise the person at 02 hour, 52 minutes, and 45 seconds?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the man who I mentioned who boasted to me. I was his platoon commander. His name is Djordje Soskic and he is from Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What is he wearing because there are two men in that frame?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah, one of them is a civilian and the other is wearing a short jacket probably from some house. It's -- we called this kind of jacket spit-fire jacket. It was called, you know. He was a soldier but he was wearing a civilian jacket over his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we tender 65 ter number 4885.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Out of abundance of caution, Ms. Biersay, which one of the two persons did the witness identify? Because that's not clear from his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist with the next exhibit, which will be 4885.2, the stills. That may assist. I wanted to freeze it here because this is actually a better image than the still I'm about to show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm sure the witness knows who he is talking about. But is the man he names the civilian or the military person with the helmet?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, the man that you named, is he on the right or the left of this frame?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the man on the right, wearing a helmet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that the man who was in -- over whom you had command, who told you about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Djordje Soskic, nicknamed Zordze, Djordje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we tender 65 ter 4885.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, with or without transcript? Because this -- this 65 ter number has both.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct. Without the transcripts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1729. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now if we could turn to 65 ter number 4885.2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, directing your attention to page 1 of this exhibit, and specifically to the left, the man that we see in that left corner, do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Predrag Miljevic, nicknamed Kinez, commander of the 1st Company of the Leva Supoderica Unit. You can see why they called him Chinaman; he has slit eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, would you be so kind as to take that electronic pen and circle the person you just described.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I think in order --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We have several more pages, but I think in order to capture the mark I'll have to tender this page now. If it works technologically, I can wait to the end as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether we are adding documents unnecessary. I mean, there's only one -- one person in the left corner of this picture. So what is the marking -- what is the use of the marking?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If the Court does not find it helpful, then I'm happy to move onto the next -- to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if we could now move to the second page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this still?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one on the far left is the man nicknamed Ceca. He was also a commander in the Leva Supoderica Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is the Trial Chamber satisfied that it's properly identified? And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here -- can I -- can I speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the far right we see again Ceca, the man from the previous picture. The one on the left is Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, wearing eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And by eyeglasses, do you mean dark glasses, sun-glasses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Milan Lancuzanin, aka Kameni. And the one on the right is the man from the previous photograph, nicknamed Ceca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in this still?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Topola. Again, I forget his real name. The man wearing this hat who's -- like has his hand on the child's head is Topola, in the centre of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could now move to the next page, please. And I know it's a bit blurry, but do you recognise anyone in this one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Djordje Soskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we tender 65 ter number 4885.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1730. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I have a clarifying question. Previously when we were discussing the -- the meetings, the briefings, held with Captain Radic, and I will read it to you. It says: "The TO is actually not the main player in war. It's the JNA. And the TO also had responsibilities toward the district and who knows what they had to do." When you say "toward the district," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say who knows what they had to do, I meant to say God knows what other duties they had. And as for the district, at that time, they had formed an autonomous district and they had their own government or a Crisis Staff, that's what I meant. They participated in the war and it's basically from that Territorial Defence that the police force was later established and the Army of the Serbian Krajina. The TO was the basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now moving to tab 99, which is 65 ter number 4809.7, and the time code runs from 00 to 3 minutes and 39 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask that the video be played. And at some point, I'm going to pause it and ask if you recognise the -- the background location.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] This is the first session of the government held in our future capital of our Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, regarding the conclusions in addition to those connected with the normalisation of life and the restoration of the normal situation. One of the basic conclusion is the prisoners, Ustashas with blood on their hands may not leave the territory of the SBWS. They cannot go to Serbia ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this I asked that the video be paused.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the background of this image?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my town, Sid. This is the municipal building. Next to it is the police building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless the street name is changed, this could be Sava Sumanovic Street or it could be Karadjordjevo Street. I haven't lived there for a long time so I don't know, but this is the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the military uniform in that still?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the TO SBWS uniform. It was the -- the green fatigues. I remember when they issued this uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd ask that we continue playing this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Reporter: ... because Serbia is a state which is not at war. Also, the troops that assisted in the capturing, they're not real soldiers, they're paramilitaries. Only our people of our Serb region which is recognised can try them. The appeals court would perhaps be at the Yugoslav level, the federal level, but the first instance trial would be here before our authorities. The agreement is with the military authorities that they would remain in some of our camps here in the vicinity of Vukovar, since one group was already taken to Sremska Mitrovica. I undertook the task to return these people, if they can be called humans at all, to return them there and to put them to trial. How do you estimate the total number of those members of the Croatian paramilitaries? We have -- hear different figures: 200 surrendered two nights ago, approximately 1 .000 today, so what numbers are we talking about? "Hadzic: I believe the number is close to 3.000, roughly 3.000 of mainly uniformed Ustashas, although there are still many hiding among the civilians. However, there are many honest people as well. Our primary task is to investigate everything and not to let anyone who is innocent get hurt or harassed. It's better to have culprit slip through than to harm somebody innocent. That is our task and we have our own legal and police authorities, so we'll work to prevent any prosecution of innocent people. "How is the establishment of the civilian rule in Vukovar going on? "Well, today was the first step. We have been prepared for this event. Unfortunately was overly optimistic thinking that Vukovar was not to devastated. Today, when I saw it, I think there no words to describe it. Literally. There is not a single undamaged house. There are even bodies still strewn in the street; thus, we first have to have our Ministry of Health and our medics or the vets prevent contagion, remove those corpses, and then we have to start normalising life. The people who carried out this fight on their backs, those are people from Petrova Gora, without them this struggle of ours for Vukovar would have been lost. I'm using this opportunity to thank them for what they've done. We've scheduled our next meeting for tomorrow with one group of ministers and the representatives of those people to find bodies to -- to found bodies, to establish civilian rule in town. It's agreed with military authorities that civilian authorities will soon take over. "Does it imply that you will take off your uniform soon? Hadzic: Well I'm the representative of the Serb people, elected by the Serbs. If the Serb people who appointed me believe that the borders are now satisfactory I will take off my uniform, but I personally believe that I should keep it on for some time yet."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, reference was made to the people from Petrova Gora. To whom do you believe this to refer to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said it: TO from Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'd ask that this clip be marked for identification. I understand that it was not in the bundle of videos yet received by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And is that why you asked it to be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1731, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether Leva Supoderica was associated with any political parties?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I just arrived, I didn't know that. However, at the lineup Kameni told us, although there was another officer who was there. I was not sure at the time who was the real commander the first two days. There was another officer, Zoran Paripovic, nicknamed Tito. The two of them were the main two. They said that most of the men were sent by the Serbian Radical Party from Serbia. I was not one of those. But I found out then that the Serbian Radical Party organised volunteer groups, and later I became myself a member of such volunteer units in other areas of Yugoslavia later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In this context I'd now like to turn to tab 93, which is 65 ter number 4760.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Before we play that video, I'd like to ask you some questions about who co-ordinated the organisation of the SRS volunteers and to send them to other areas. Do you recall who in the SRS was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, at the HQ of the party in Belgrade, there was a Crisis Staff during the war. And in that Crisis Staff there was Zoran Drazilovic and Ljubisa Petkovic. Ljubisa Petkovic, I believe, was the head of the Crisis Staff and he was the co-ordinator. He organised the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe to the -- the -- the Trial Chamber how they were actually moved from Belgrade to other places where they were deployed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, you go to Belgrade, to that Crisis Staff, and then a file is opened for you; that is to say, if you are a new-comer. They take your ID and they take down your personal data, including specific features, such as birth marks, tattoos, et cetera, and from there you go to Bubanj Potok which is the barracks of the JNA near Belgrade, and there we undergo a short training. We get equipment and weapons. And from there, I departed twice from that same place, we went through the airport, and from there to the Banja Luka airport and the Bihac airport. That's how we travelled. Sometimes we travelled by bus to Herzegovina. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now turning to tab 93, 65 ter number 4760.1. And my intention is to play the -- the clip, and perhaps towards the end I will stop it to ask you if you recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Well, good look. Maybe a good mediator for these conflicts would be if not Arkan then, for example, Dr. Vojislav Seselj, president of the Serbian Radical Party. He has not reached Mostar yet, but today he stayed on Mount Romanija. "Reporter: On the first day of the referendum Dr. Vojislav Seselj, the Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda and the president of the Serbian Radical Party, arrived today in Republika Srpska. As soon as he arrived he crossed the Drina river, he went to visit our defenders on the first line of defence. Afterwards, he visited Knezina, a village and monastery in free Serbian Romanija, the oath of the new Serbian Chetnik Vojvodas. "Unknown man: Order number 124. As the only Chetnik Vojvoda directly engaged in the present-day struggle for the liberation of the Serbian people and following the tradition of Serbian Chetniks, for exceptional achievements in this war, great heroism, and proven arts of war of the most distinguished Chetnik commanders I hereby pronounce ... "Report: Romanija, a mountain that does not speak to its enemies, rejoiced at the oath of 18 new Vojvodas, an oath it had not heard for 50 years. "The Vojvodas: I swear as the Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I ask that the video be paused, Mr. Stoparic, and referring to your statement in paragraph 5, you described that there were 19 SRS Vojvodas and you describe what was required in order to become a Vojvoda that you had to have 500 volunteers under your control. Is this consistent with the proclamations of the Vojvodas that you describe in your statement in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that figure, 500, from Kameni when he became a Vojvoda. He was saying that there should be no less than 500 volunteers so that they can be raised at any time. But Seselj did not give this title only to commanders. Also to politicians, people from the Crisis Staff, including the Ljubisa Petkovic and the current present of Serbia, Tomislav Nikolic. Not all of those who received the title had been in the war. Some of them would not survive two minutes of combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Seselj's opinion, they deserve it for other reasons. Here on the photo we see Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you're specifically discussing 1 minute and 27 seconds. And what -- where is Kameni?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre. He is holding the candle lower than the men around him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair hair. Not one with the dark hair, the one with fair hair.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was he named as a Vojvoda before or after Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before Vukovar. Nobody was given the title before. It was after. First of all, they had to deserve this honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could please continue the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Seselj I swear to God and Saint Sava. "The men repeat. "Seselj: That I will fight with all my might for the freedom of the Serbian people. "The men repeat. "Seselj: And the restoration of a unified Serbian state in the Balkans which will encompass all Serbian lands. "The men repeat the oath. "Seselj: So God help me. "Amen. "Good luck and bless you. May God give you a long life. "Reporter: One can trust, then, that it's indeed going to be so. The rank of Chetnik Vojvoda was bestowed on these Serbian heros from all Serbian areas: Zdravko Abramovic; Branislav Vakic; Srecko Radovanovic; Slavko Crnic; Nedeljko Vidakovic; Slavko Aleksic; Mitar Maksimovic, Manda; Miroslav Vukovic, Cele; Milika Dacevic, Ceko; Tomislav Nikolic; Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni; Zoran Drazinovic, Cica; Jovo Ostojic; Ljubisa Petkovic; Todor Lazic; Mirko Blagojevic; Dragan Cvetkovic; and Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne." 1

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to Kameni, did you recognise anybody else in that video we just saw?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many. Apart from Seselj there was Drazilovic, Ljubisa Petkovic, Tomislav Nikolic, those who I know by name. Then Vojvoda Manda from Ugljevik, then the one from Sarajevo. I recognise all of them. I just can't give you their names now. Later on I saw them in various theatres of war. Others were very often on television. Blagojevic was there. Mirko from Bijeljina. Then Branislav Lakic from Nis. I recognised many of them. But they are wearing those long beards and they're all -- they all look the same in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the Vukovar operations, which ones did you recognise from that specific operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kameni. Although some other Vojvodas said later they had been at Vukovar. Maybe. But not in my sector. Even the one from Nis, the Vojvoda from Nis. He was also in Vukovar. But out of all those radicals, Kameni was the main one for me. He was my commander but also a better man, as far as I'm concerned. And I knew him better.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we tender 65 ter number 4760.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1732. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I do see the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Stoparic, this is the moment we take the first break. We will be back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, I understand that the Registrar has now received the CD containing the clip for MFI 1731, and so I believe now it can receive an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That will be 1731 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Registrar. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm hoping that the remaining of my questions will take about 20 minutes or so. I want to quickly talk about Velepromet, then move to a brief discussion on the Skorpions, and then I will show you a video, so that's where I'm going. In your 2003 statement in paragraph 38, you mentioned that you had not heard of a meeting held at Velepromet in which Goran Hadzic participated, and my question to you is: Did you ever have occasion to see anyone connected with the SBWS government in Velepromet, in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The question is vague.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, I suppose we could see if the witness understood it, and I'm happy to clarify, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Would you be more precise, the question would become leading, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stoparic, did you ever see any representatives of the SBWS government in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the TO commanders and the like. But as for government officials, I didn't really know them all. I would have recognised Goran Hadzic if I had seen him. Filipovic, Grahovac too, and another man I would certainly recognise but I forget his name. I did go to Velepromet to get cigarettes and movement permits in the area of combat activity and permits to leave Vukovar, but I don't really remember seeing any one of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there an office for the SBWS government in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I don't know. There was some warehouses there. There were soldiers and the TO. Probably some civil administration, too. But if it was the government or whether it was administration at town level, there were various people. There was even a kitchen. Some sort of administration, yes, but I'm not sure about the level they were at. I'm speaking about the period of combat activity. I don't know about any later time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. I'd now like to move to your time at Djeletovci with the Skorpions, and very briefly could you describe to the Trial Chamber what armed force -- to what armed force the Skorpions belonged? I know there's a complex history but if you could just make it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially speaking, the Skorpions were part of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The commander was General Loncar, or Loncarevic. There were also security forces from Serbia who came in often and people were trained there. There were security structures, the police, and we even had a working relationship with the oil industry of Krajina. Once I received an envelope from them with German marks, then some money went to Belgrade in Yugoslav dinars, and I also received money from a third source, that's the commander, or sometimes he would give me petrol, a barrel or two, or other times he would give me German marks. It was complicated. The basic task at the Djeletovci base was holding our position. There was the Bosut river and that was a natural border between the then-district of SBWS and the rest of Croatia, and we protected the oil terminal there. And our secondary tasks were connected with our going to Bosnia-Herzegovina. But after the Skorpions were disbanded and then we gathered again, we even went to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 72 of your statement. You talked about the Tigers being based in Erdut and the Red Berets, the JSO, being in Ilok, and the Skorpions in Djeletovci. Who was in charge of the Tigers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan. And the JSO, they were at Ilok, in a wine cellar in the direction of Sid called Pajzos. They had a base there, too. It was on the very border between Serbia and Croatia. Pajzos is situated on the very border, so a part of the base would be in Serbia and another part in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Stoparic, for the benefit of the transcript, could you repeat the last thing that you said. You were discussing Pajzos being on the very border, partly in Serbia and another part in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the members of the JSO were or whatever they called themselves at the time because they were changing names. JSO was the last name. And their commander was Franko Simatovic, and they were directly under the state security administration. They were part of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe also in paragraph 72: "We were all" -- "we were all right along the border with Serbia." Why was the deployment concentrated along the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- actually, it wasn't an observation of mine. I heard it from people. Because you can always go into action, leave fast, and return fast. Their actions probably weren't public.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "leave fast and return fast," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because you can never say that the unit belongs to SBWS. They're in Serbia and officially they don't take part in the war activities. That's where they were along the border. Ilok itself is a town in Croatia. On the other side of the river, there's Backa Palanka in Serbia. And the Skorpions went a bit deeper.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, have you ever met Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice. At two different periods. Once I met him when he came to visit us. We were in an improvised base near Gospic. And the second time it was in the surroundings of Livno in a nearby village. Mount Dinara, that region. That's where I saw him for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to play a video and ask you if you recognise any of the speakers. And I'm now moving to tab 98, which is 65 ter number 4990.2. And, for the record, it's from 1 hour, 1 minute, and 1 second, to 1 hour, 2 minute, and 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to -- we did deliver some transcripts and I'm wondering -- I just wanted to confirm if the interpreters have the transcript pertaining to this video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have just found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So at this time we'll begin from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Anyway, the questions are becoming more specific: Did Arkan attend the government session where the minister of defence was discussed? In which capacity? Who brought his unit and is his unit for combat or for creating public order and peace? "Answer: This is a string of questions. I can answer all. Indeed, Arkan was present at the government session. And before the beginning of the government session everyone knows I requested that only the ministers be present because we were discussing important issues, but the prime minister replied telling me that if I met Mr. Raznjatovic, he was a member of the government. I was astonished and asked if we was with internal affairs or defence. I didn't know. I made a small joke. No, he said, he's the special advisor to President Hadzic. President Hadzic himself confirmed that he was a special advisor and that he was entitled to attend this session. All I could do was go along with it. As far as his volunteer units are concerned, they're welcome in the Republic of Serbian Krajina to fight same as all the other volunteers."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the image that is on your screen, Mr. Stoparic, do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time we'd move for admission of 65 ter 5990.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because there is no nexus between the statement of Mr. Martic and witness evidence. And for the purpose of recognition, video still is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Our position is that the witness has spoken about Arkan Tigers when in Djeletovci in 1993. And here we have Milan Martic, a man whom he's met, who he recognises, who is speaking about the connection between Goran Hadzic and Arkan. So we believe it's directly relevant to the topics covered in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But there was no nexus between evidence of this witness and the -- the statement about relations between Goran Hadzic and Milan Martic from this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Ms. Biersay, you'll have to try to get this one in through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you spent 1991 to 1997 in the various armed forces throughout the former Yugoslavia. How does Vukovar stand out in your total war experience?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's no secret. This was the first serious experience. Tovarnik was my first action, but it doesn't carry such weight. Vukovar was worst. When I went to Bosnia and the local commanders would learn that I was a veteran of the Vukovar theatre, they would always treat me with respect. Vukovar was worst. Even in Kosovo while NATO was bombing, it wasn't so bad as in Vukovar. Or perhaps it's just my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter number 5977, the 2003 statement, as well as 5976, which is the addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object because this statement is incomplete because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which one, the first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 5977. Because the witness gave additions to his statement on 10 December 2003, and he gave many corrections and clarifications of this particular statement in approximately more than 20 paragraphs. So I see it is -- it was not addressed by the Prosecution. And I have only -- it is in our tab, Defence tab 4, I only have a redacted version of these additions, and I don't know whether the witness signed these additions or not but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The first question regarding corrections and additions, the witness addressed all additions -- all corrections in the -- which is 65 ter number 5976, they were tendered together in the Stanisic and Simatovic case without tendering the -- the material that Mr. Zivanovic is discussing, which was not signed by the witness as our record indicates, and he has made his fresh corrections to the -- the statement here in this courtroom. Now, are there topics that were addressed in either -- in subsequent statements? Yes. But are we seeking to elicit those additional bits of information? No, we're not. And so we think, as far as the accuracy of his statement, it is it now accurate as he has described it to the Trial Chamber with what he has described in this courtroom and with the addendum. And that's how they also proceeded in the Stanisic and Simatovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The rest seems to be material eventually for cross-examination, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll use it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement under 65 ter number 5977 shall be assigned Exhibit P1733. And the addendum with the 65 ter number 5976 shall be assigned Exhibit P1734. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that concludes my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Biersay. Mr. Zivanovic, when you -- when you use that other statement or those corrections, I would remind you of our practice not to admit other statements. So if you use it, you'll read it into the record. So -- the questions you ask will comprise what is -- whatever is in -- in those -- in those corrections, and we'll get the answers from the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll comply with your orders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Stoparic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I am the Defence counsel of Goran Hadzic in this trial. I will start with what we spoke about just now. I have a Prosecution document dated 10 December 2003 entitled annex to your statement of your -- of the 21st to 24th December -- or November 2002. It's document number 1D322. I only have the English version. I don't know if it was translated. But let me ask you if you remember that in December 2003, you spoke to representatives of the OTP about your statement that you gave from the 21st to the 24th of November, which you also spoke about and had an opportunity to read it. Do you remember that you spoke to them; and did you then clarify or correct some things in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember each and every conversation, but if you scroll down and if I see the names of the investigators, I'm sure I'll remember. I mean, I do remember but I would remember more easily if could I see the names of the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The names are mentioned here are Gerry Sexton and Dorian Barag. Do you remember this interview? I'm not going to ask you about each and every paragraph. I'll limit myself to some things that are interesting to us and concern your statement. First of all, I'm interested in the correction to paragraph 4. I'll read it out to you in English and you will then hear: [In English] "I don't know exactly when the TO SBWS office in Sid was opened, but I'm sure it was after May 1991 and the events in Borovo Selo."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm having a problem with my microphone, I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Probably my fault again, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This one seems to be working. I -- I rise just to say that I have a B/C/S version, I believe, of this document, which I'd like to have the record reflect is an internal memorandum which is why it was redacted because it was not a witness statement reviewed by the witness but meant for internal purposes. I'm happy to give this to either Mr. Zivanovic or to the witness, if it would assist either one of them, as it is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it will be very helpful, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So I think perhaps for the witness, it may be best. Now I think it is, as it is in B/C/S, I -- I think that's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to explain what I meant by this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Or, in other words, since it differs from paragraph 4 in your statement because I believe you said there that the office was opened in May 1991. Now you said that it was actually after the events in May, so it may have been another month. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I learned of the existence of that office after May. I don't know the exact date, but I am convinced that I only learned of it after May. It may have been in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see in paragraph 6 of your statement, you explained precisely what you've just discussed, not in the document you were just given but in paragraph 6 of your statement. That's P5977. You explained here that they asked you to produce your military service book and if you happened to have a war-time assignment written in there, you would not have been accepted as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me on what basis do you know that you would not be eligible as a volunteer in that case. Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to that office. I hadn't taken with me my military service book, only my ID, and the man turned me back and said that I should bring my military service book. And he told me that the Yugoslav People's Army doesn't know when they would call up -- whether they would call me up into the reserve. They had their system of war-time assignments. They could call me up at any time if I had a war-time assignment. However, I didn't have one. And then the man said if the army did not assign you in advance as a reserve, then we can accept you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing from your experience and the experience from other men you knew, was it a requirement to be accepted as a volunteer to have done your military service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the TO of SBWS, I'll explain to you what the rules were. They did their job very professionally. They wanted you to produce your military service book and they complied with all the military regulations of the JNA. Later on, things changed. Among the Seselj's volunteers in Bosnia, there were people who had never served in the army, et cetera. However, in this office where this man Filipovic worked, he wanted to be sure that you didn't have a war-time assignment because if you had one then the army could call you up at any time as a reservist. I was accepted because I did not have a war-time assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that later on they started inducting everyone including people who did not -- who never served in the army, et cetera, that was later in 1992, right, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that did not happen in the district. In the district there was no more war after Vukovar. These things happened later where there was absolutely no control. In the district it was according to the rules. I had to produce my military service book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now would you please look at your statement, paragraph 7. This same statement, paragraph 7, where it says that your status as a volunteer lasted for one week. And after that, you got a military call-up paper from the JNA. You said you were required to report to the 1st Guards Brigade. However, yesterday you corrected it and said it was the Kraljevo Brigade not the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not correct that. You want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just wait for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about that first week or perhaps ten days. I focussed on the one week, the first week when I was a member of the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and the main commander for us was the Kraljevo Brigade. After that, we went to Lipovaca, where from we would go later on to Vukovar. That's when Mr. Grahovac came. And he said that this Kraljevo Brigade would no longer be there. Instead a Guards Brigade from Belgrade will be coming. And those who want to go on in the war would be under the Guards Brigade from Belgrade. He listed us all, and he said that we would get official summons at our home address. And after the war, I went home and, indeed, they delivered this summons by courier service. And later on, we were under the Guards Brigade. And officially we would have been reservists of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify one thing. When you say that your status as volunteer lasted approximately one week, which period would that be? Do you count from the moment when you reported to the Territorial Defence in Sid and the week after, or some other period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I counted from the day when we departed for Tovarnik and until Djeletovci. Now, within the first three days when we got equipment and weapons, it took us two or three days to form platoons, to clean our weapons, so I was there in this base in -- in Tovarnik. I believe one week passed between that and Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were there in that period when the action took place in Tovarnik. And during those days, your unit was subordinated to the Kraljevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a motorised brigade. It probably had a number, but I don't remember it. Yes, we were there. We were subordinated to them. Their officers were in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's, in fact, a JNA unit.
