utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because on page 6 there is an omission, because you said not Kraljevo Brigade. You said Kraljevska Brigada and it was interpreted as "Royal Brigade." Just tell me one more thing. Before you departed for Vukovar, you received an official military call-up from the JNA to report to that Guards Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I was already in Vukovar. But when I returned from Vukovar, from the war, when I returned home, my brother showed me that paper. However, at Lipovaca I had already signed some paper and Grahovac required us to sign it. He said you are not cannon fodder. You have certain legal rights as volunteers. You know that volunteers and reservists have the same status. The only difference is that reservists were called up, and volunteers volunteered. But legally we had the same rights. The same status.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that's in fact what you said in this addendum to your statement. We can go back to 1D322. That's what you were just given in the B/C/S version. It says: "The call-up papers from the JNA were delivered by courier service." Can you read this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it says here by post.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in the other paper it says by courier service.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's usually the courier service and Sid has one. They deal with these things because the post does not always work perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say here that, on this basis, you were on an equal footing with all the other reservists of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I received my salary for the service in Vukovar from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you named the person from whom you received your salary. You said you were given it at the barracks of the 1st Guards Brigade, but I think in para 23, in the last paragraph, you gave the name of the officer from whom you received your salary. It's the last paragraph because paragraph 23 has two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I rise because I'm getting a bit lost in which document we're talking about. When you say in -- you said in paragraph -- Mr. Zivanovic, paragraph 23, in which -- which document are we?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it's now the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would be assisted if perhaps when you're referring to it to say memorandum just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- just to keep it -- it would just assist the record and me trying to find which section you're discussing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that correct? Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Captain Zirojevic. I asked for him. He came out and he sent me to a warrant officer whose name I don't know. The warrant officer gave me a certificate and he paid out my salary on the basis of that certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you stated that when you volunteered you were issued the old-type JNA uniform. Was that uniform significantly different from the uniforms of reservists?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I explain this? The old uniform is the sturdy, very warm uniform. The reservists' uniforms were the same but made of a different fabric. But they were basically the same. The camouflage uniforms were not common at that time, although I later received at Velepromet a camouflage uniform consisting of the top and the bottoms, and the hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the time when you volunteered. Was it -- was the difference between those two uniforms very -- very obvious so that you could easily tell reservists from soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were, if I can say, tongue and cheek, we were all like Easter eggs. Reservists usually had their uniforms ready and they kept them at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement, and you mentioned today in your testimony, two names. The first one was Slobodan Grahovac. You were shown a document -- maybe I'll show it again to you later. I'd like to know, because I believe you said he had some connection to the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Do you know this first-hand or did you hear it from someone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature on that document is Filipovic's, not Grahovac. I remember when I came to the office of that man, Filipovic, I believe his name was Dusan, I used to see him on TV even back in Sid, he was something in that government. I don't know what exactly. But maybe I'm mistaken. I believe that he was some sort of minister or something. Or he -- he became a minister later, unless I'm very confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking. It's in paragraph 19 of your statement. Although you amended it later in the memorandum. I'm asking you this because our information is that Slobodan Grahovac played absolutely no part in the government of SBWS at the time when it was a district or at the time when it was the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That's the reason why I'm asking, because in paragraph 19 of the memorandum, the document you're looking at, you said that he was presented to you as the minister of defence of SAO Krajina. My question is: Who presented him or who introduced him to you as the minister of defence, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember his face very clearly. He was wearing the same uniform, those same fatigues, and that's the first time in my life that I saw a Heckler gun. There were two instructors there, one from Backa Palanka and the other one was nicknamed Djani, I don't know from where, and they introduced him to us. I know that after the war, this Grahovac worked in the customs service or maybe in the state security, and there was a report that he was hurt or killed in a traffic accident. But from that time, I remember that he was presented to us as a minister. Even the defence minister. But that is not necessarily correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at P1727. That is the document which bears Filipovic's signature. I see that he signed this on behalf of the chief. I don't know whether he was the chief or somebody else was the chief because we have different information about him too. If we could just see the top of the B/C/S version. I'm interested in this date, 18 October 1991. There is a stamp on the left-hand side. What does this mean? What is written in the centre, OP and then STO. We know that STO is the Territorial Defence Staff. But what is OP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative maybe ... I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's all right. I'm asking you because we know about the so-called TO Staff of Vukovar from all the documents we have seen, and we know of another staff, or other headquarters in Vukovar. You mentioned Vujovic and Vujanovic and we have information about the fact that the previous commander was Dusan Jaksic. So I wanted to see if we could clarify this matter, whether these were two distinct staffs or maybe the same staff in two places at various times or maybe one subordinated to the other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there had to be a staff. In Vukovar it's a town staff, and certainly there must have been one for the whole district, but I really don't know how they were connected and whether they co-operated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to see the bottom of the document because there's a name there. Can you read this name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Ceprnja. I heard of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before the war he also worked at the Vukovar TO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. But that name did pop up. I mean, there, on the front line. I believe that he even supplied some stuff to us, such as cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you first meet Milan Lancuzanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were lined up on that occasion. When I came from Lipovaca. I first met him and that man Ubi [as interpreted] Paripovic. Although, I know that he was in Tovarnik too, but I don't remember him from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was in Vukovar. So I met him in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that later he called you often because he fell ill and asked you for assistance. So it is my impression that you grew quite close, that you were good mates.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- actually, I built his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that after the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, after the war in this district of ours. Later on, there was also the war in Kosovo. But it was around 2000 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that up until the war, he lived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I also know his father and his brother. I was in his house in Vukovar. It's in Leva Supoderica. I also went to his father's place who lived by Novi Sad. I forget exactly where. And I was -- I was at his brother's house and know his wife and her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know that when the war broke out, he and his family fled Vukovar and went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was returning to Vukovar the same way as I went there, through Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean he was returning as a volunteer; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a volunteer or TO. Anyway, a member of the armed forces. What exactly he was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you know that he was also at Tovarnik involved in the activities around Tovarnik, although you didn't meet him then.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he returned to Vukovar, when arrived there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found him in Vukovar when I arrived there, so I wouldn't know. He may have told me, but I didn't -- I don't remember. Anyway, he came there before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because according to the information that I have, on this very day indicated here, the 18th of October, he arrived Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. Or, rather, I'm not really convinced ... maybe -- maybe earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had been appointed commander of the 1st Platoon in this Leva Supoderica Unit. And you said that on the 20th of November, you were the duty officer at headquarters. I would like to know whether these duty shifts were a common thing in the Leva Supoderica unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there would always be duty shifts. When the commander was there, he had certain people who dealt with some matters. I was a platoon commander and I was more in charge of hands-on stuff. There were also the communications there, and the staffs, so if Radic or Zirojevic came, somebody had to be there to call in the commander if he is out on the front line. You understand? It's normal procedure anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And according to the rules that was an officer, so -- or not a private, such as probably a company commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And, as a rule, they were locals, from Vukovar. The -- they were familiar with the terrain. I was duty officer only once because nobody else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that before that you were never duty officer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did stay at the staff sometimes overnight, when we knew that there was no activity planned, but it was not a usual thing to have me there. I remember this instance because it took so long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in something else. We'll get back to this specific instance. I would like to know what you, as duty officer, but I'm not referring specifically to the day when the Ovcara events happened, but more generally, in principle, what were your duties? What were you supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not allow everybody to enter. When somebody comes with some request, asking for cigarettes or ammunition or something, then you go to the warehouse. You issue ammunition or Zoljas. And if there's an incident, such as a row, you take care of it. If somebody drinks alcohol, these were the things you would deal with. And the usual staff affairs, so you don't decide about anything. You don't take any decisions. And when there are people you don't know, you have to ask who they are and where they were going. It's something like a sentry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also had means of communication, such as a Motorola and an induction telephone.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And a power generator and a battery-powered TV set because the houses we were staying at didn't have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This induction telephone, is that a land-line telephone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have to lay a phone line from point A to point B, and then -- that's how it works. But it's the worst communications line because these wires can break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it's the safest.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, according to military doctrine, courier communication is safest. But these were -- this was the hardware that the JNA had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this: When you were duty officer, did you have communication with other units, such as JNA units or other units in that sector?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two documents. One was a list of codes. So when you set up a communication, then you use these code-names and people would understand. So it wasn't a very long list of codes, but there were -- there was a number of codes anyway. It was line communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing: The duty officer, did he make notes of the events during his duty shift?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You would brief the commander orally if there was an incident. If there was none, nothing. You must understand that we didn't become officers by attending Military Academy. We didn't have much paperwork. We were more or less self-proclaimed. The army did accept my rank eventually, but when I served in the army, I didn't attend the reserve officers' school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the duty shifts, how long were they roughly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your shift was either a day-time shift or a night-time shift. But, on that day Kameni had gone are all the mainly officers and just said I should stay on duty. Although there were the squad commanders there, so I don't know why they didn't do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So, roughly speaking, a duty shift would last up to 12 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A regular duty shift, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking because many things can happen in 12 hours, so it is probably more convenient to write things down because it's easy to forget things so you wouldn't be able to brief the commander.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When somebody called, you make a note of it. And the line wasn't used for private conversations anyway. So if anybody called and the commander was out, and I must tell you that Kameni was not self-proclaimed guy. He was a brave man. And we didn't use Motorolas often in some periods because anybody can listen in. In that case, you go to the other person in person. But I didn't use these means of communication so often because I was a combat man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During these duty shifts was there communication with other units, such as these assault groups of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I don't know everything about being a duty officer. It happened by chance that I was duty officer on that unfortunate day, and I didn't know about Ovcara. I only learned about it later. There was this man by the name of Slobodan Katic. Whenever he was present he was at the communications centre, so he was best informed about who was doing what and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. What was Katic's job in your unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a kind of officer but he didn't have any subordinates. He didn't have a platoon. He considered himself assistant commander. He was a radical from Belgrade. He was very active in the Radical Party, and, in that sense, he was in contact with them. When I joined the unit, I had no idea it had anything to do with a political party. Only later did they start distributing applications to join the party, and Katic was something like a political figure, and he was Kameni's friend, whether he -- they went back a long time or not, I don't know. But when they were there, they socialised a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now go into your clarifications about Tovarnik. You said that you saw many corpses at Tovarnik on the street or in the gardens and you supposed that they were Croats because they were not buried. Maybe due to the fighting, even if those dead bodies were Serbian bodies, they couldn't be buried because of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the one woman was Serbian. There may have been some Serbian dead bodies among the ones I saw, but the ones on the tarmac certainly were not Serbian bodies. The military police guarded them. And I saw two murders with my own eyes, and I know that they weren't Serbs. One man's name was Mate, I think. He was killed by Zeljko Krnjajic. And his wife was killed by Predrag. One of them is now being tried for Lovas and the other is at large. They killed this married couple personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also say that the military police was guarding a couple of Croatian bodies near the petrol station. Why do you believe that those were Croat bodies?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the second day. All the Serbs who had fled had returned by that time. And if those bodies were from a Serb family, the families would have picked them up. We also didn't find anyone in Ilaca. Everybody had fled. We didn't find anybody. We did not have to fight apart in the artillery preparation before we went in. That's why I believe that they were Croats. Or perhaps other non-Serbs. Because if it was somebody whose family was around, they would have been collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because the other bodies were not guarded by the military police. Did it perhaps occur to you that the military police was guarding Serb bodies until they are collected?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're driving at. It would have been a possibility but for the fact that on the first day when I was at the same place, there were no bodies, and the next day there was not a single Croat soldier in that area who would have killed those Serbs. They may have been victims of a general crime. It was complete chaos, anarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it perhaps your impression that the military police was guarding bodies in order to secure a -- an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been possible. That would have been the most realistic option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break: Do you know what Zeljko Krnjajic did before the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war? I don't know. After the war, he was a police officer in Sid. He even served in Kosovo as a policeman. But before the war, I don't know. I had contacts with him and talked with him because he also bought a house in the Sid municipality, in Asica village, and I went there because we knew each other from the time when he was my commander. But he never mentioned what he did before the war. I believe he comes originally from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that he was a policeman even before the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You see, after that brief war in Tovarnik, he became the commander of the police because the police force was formed and the civilian administration immediately after. And if he had, indeed, been a policeman before the war and graduated from the police academy, now I understand why he was named police commander. But one thing is sure: He was in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, in his own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My information is exactly the opposite. He may have said that but ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. That's what he told us. Because he had a camouflage uniform on when we were in Sid and were receiving weapons he and Vojkapic were the only ones who had experience and the only experience could have been Borovo Selo, and said that he was in Borovo Selo himself unless he was in the Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is, indeed, Mr. Zivanovic. We will take the break until 12.45, Mr. Stoparic. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were talking about the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, do you know who, in fact, was the commander of that Territorial Defence at the time when you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I heard later that it was General Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "General Badza," do you mean Radovan Stojicic, nicknamed Badza?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know roughly where he was working, what was he -- his other job at the time, from which structures he came?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was part of the special units of the state security of the Republic of Serbia, the so-called SAJ. I don't know his entire career, but, for a while, he was there too. I don't know the rest. I first heard of the man when there was a strike in some mine and he went to deal with it with his special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were speaking about Slobodan Grahovac, you said that, to the best of your knowledge, he was also a member of the police. Did you mean the police of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war in Vukovar, yes, that's what I heard. Or perhaps I heard it on radio or television. I'm not sure whether it was the police or the state security. I'm a bit confused. Maybe he was in the customs service, also. I don't know all the places where he worked afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just be clear: Are you talking about Serbia or the Republic of the Serbian Krajina where he worked in the police or the state security or the customs service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia was still part of the federal state, along with Montenegro. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't mean Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because we have information --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I refer to the page 613, lines 16 to 19, there Grahovac -- [Interpretation] that Grahovac was the Chief of Staff in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. What remained in my head was that he was some minister. But sometimes you get confused about these things. You take a lie for the truth, sometimes you are given misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe he was falsely presented to you. I'm just saying we don't have information that he was a minister in the government.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not introduce himself as such. Other people said he was a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you said that before coming into the courtroom, you had read this statement you have before you. That's 5977, with the corrigendum 5976. And you said that to the best of your knowledge it's all true and accurate when you were asked so by the Prosecutor. I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 36 in that statement. You will see soon the B/C/S version on the screen too. What we see here is the same thing you said in your testimony, that you personally had not been at Ovcara but you know certain details about the killings committed there and that, on that day, Kameni, Ceca, Kinez, and Djo went to the war staff of the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade. However, you say here in your statement: "They returned around noon." And today, you said they returned that evening when it was already dark. Since you said yesterday you had read your statement and you stood by it and your testimony today was different on this point, I'd like to know if you can explain this.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These words "around noon" don't have to be correct. It could have been 1.00 p.m. I'm not sure whether it was 12.00 or 1.00 p.m. But I spoke to Kameni on the Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, around 12.00 or 1.00 p.m., you spoke to him. Does it mean you talked to him in person or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just spoke to him. He asked me, in fact, he said, I know you've been there a long time, but stay on some longer. And they returned into the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, in your statement, in the sentence after that, it says: "I was the duty officer. When Kameni and the others came back from Belgrade I noticed that they were very anxious ..." So I want to know if you did not see them around noon when they returned, how were you able to notice that they were anxious?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I spoke to him around noon, and when he returned that evening, in my mind, he had returned from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that they were anxious at that time? Did they all come back together, the four of them, or just Kameni?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them. Well, I was able to see that they were nervous, worried. He asked very briskly that we establish our manning strength, and we had been in combat together. I was able to see that he was anxious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, you say in the next sentence: "Kameni said they were going to find Miroljub."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So when did he go to find Miroljub? That evening or that day at noon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to quote Kameni, to quote what he said when I received my task to establish the manning strength. He also said, You don't have to go find Miroljub yourself. I'll go. From the moment when we spoke on the Motorola until they returned, I don't know what, in the meantime, was going on with Miroljub. Later on, it turned out that Miroljub was with them. I don't know why he had to go find Miroljub. He was furious with that Miroljub.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, try to explain to me why did he say, Don't go look for Miroljub. Why would you look for Miroljub in the first place? At least that's what it says in the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that to me. He said they would go to find Miroljub.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say why?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably did, but I had already left to establish the manning strength. They stayed behind. And when I came back, there were many more people there. I asked him, What's going on? What's all the commotion about? And he said, Something is going on that shouldn't be happening. He didn't say, Something happened. He said, Something is going on that shouldn't be happening. And the next day, it was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's very important what you say here. In the next sentence already it says when they left for Ovcara to look for Miroljub, they remained there for two or two and a half hours, and when they returned to the command, they ordered you to go to the unit urgently and find out where everyone is. From your statement, it follows that they went to Ovcara and stayed there for two or two and a half hours, returned, and it was then that Kameni gave you the order to find out where the troops from your unit were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kameni told me himself that they had been at Ovcara for a while. And that's certainly true. There's no need for him to lie. After Ovcara, they came to headquarters. That's true as well. Whether or not they went to see Miroljub again, I don't know. They said they would. I may have mixed things up when I made my statement. I -- sometimes we -- I spoke from memory, and sometimes I said what we agreed I would say at Zemun in case we were questioned about Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a word, what we read in paragraph 36 is partly untrue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained. When I spoke I amalgamated both versions into one. That's why there's a problem, not only with you but also with the Prosecutor. Things had to be clarified for the Prosecution too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're aware that you're giving evidence under oath. Did Kameni go to find Miroljub, as you say in your statement, around noon when he arrived and stayed for two or two and a half hours and gave you that order, or did he set out to find Miroljub in the evening hours, and Vujovic too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him in the evening, he said that he would go to find Miroljub. And before that, he was there as well. I don't know whether he actually went there at night. And, frankly speaking, I asked him that after the war, and he answered, yes, that is -- yes, I saw things but I didn't kill anyone, and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I find that understandable if you went there around noon or within those two and a half hours he stayed, nothing was happening of that kind. But when he went there in the evening, then the situation was quite different. That's why I'm asking you whether he went there around noon, the way it says in your statement, or if he went there in the evening -- actually, he arrived in the evening and after that went there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The real truth is that we spoke around noon or 1.00 and that he came in in the evening and -- well, the evening. I don't know. It may have been around 6.00 or maybe even 5.00 because it was winter time. And he ordered me to establish the manning strength and that he would go to find Miroljub. Whether he actually did, I don't know. He says he didn't. When he went there, I don't know. Perhaps it was a scheme to confuse me. It was suspicious to me when he ordered me to establish the manning strength because that was the first time ever since we arrived to -- at Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, this part of your statement where you say that Kameni arrived at noon with these four -- or with these three members of your unit is not true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he arrived in Vukovar around noon because we spoke by means of our communication lines, and I saw him in person in the evening. That's to the best of my recollection. They also confused me with their -- with those meetings we had. What should we say, and, you know, that stuff, unfortunately. So I got confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 5979.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this text?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my handwriting. Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us when this was drafted? There's no date here.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in 2004. Or 2005 maybe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here in this statement, you speak about the meeting you had with Kameni and three other former members of that unit. Tell me how long after that meeting did you draft this statement? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over a year, I think. Well, no, not really. Maybe even two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody ask you to write this statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigator, I think. I can give you the name, if necessary. Paolo Pastore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a closer look at this statement. Let's start with paragraph 1. It says that before the investigation in Serbia, you met Lancuzanin and that he invited you to meet Ceca and Kinez as well. Tell me, how come people knew that there would be an investigation in Serbia on the -- about this event? Because 12 years or who knows how much had elapsed.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but Kameni knew. He must have learned that from someone from security service. When we went to those interviews, I couldn't suggest them what to do because I wasn't there with them. But later on, people were brought in some six months or so later because I know that Kinez came to Sid after he had been interviewed in Belgrade on which occasion he had to take a lie detector test.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you meet to discuss these things?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we went to Mitrovica to Ceca's place and then went to Ruma to Kinez's place, and then we also spoke in the railway station bar. And after some time we went to Belgrade, all of us together, and met Djo. There was also an attorney and some other people I don't know. And there was a man who was at the TO at the time. His nickname was Djani. Actually, it was either he or a relative of his, because that Djani lived abroad for a while. And then Kinez came to see us once, because I told you that I was one of the -- the people who built Kameni's house and we were just finishing a part of the work, I remember. He had already been brought in by the police and had to take the lie detector test, and then he would tell us how he faired. Later Kameni also was summoned. In Sid, there were inspectors that came for him. At the time, Kameni also was interviewed by ICTY investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Kameni was interviewed by ICTY investigators. Is that what he told you or did he hear that from the -- from Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. I actually escorted him when he was going there, and he took an attorney with him because he was a suspect. And when he returned from Belgrade, I think that he even told me that the interview had been videotaped. Nobody told me here. He told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you met once when Kameni said that there would be an investigation. Then you met once in Belgrade when that Djani was present, and that you met once when Kinez took the lie detector test, and once later, when Kameni went to be interviewed by ICTY investigators. That was four times?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I met Kameni daily. Almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to these four situations, not your daily meetings with Kameni. Did you speak about the events at Ovcara on each of these four occasions? Did you consult as to what you should say once the investigation begins?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Kameni went to be interviewed by the investigators, we didn't discuss that. But, otherwise, yes, we spoke about Ovcara. We spoke about Sljivancanin. We even called him from the cafe. There was a special system in place. You -- you had -- we called him and wait for three rings and only then would he answer the phone. He hadn't been arrested yet. We all liked the man; Sljivancanin I mean. The Prosecutors once told me that they wanted me to testify in his trial but I refused. However, they didn't insist. There was no way of making me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They would have been able to make me testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about Ovcara, why was it necessary to communicate with Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak to him. They spoke to him on the phone. But when they did, they only said hello. They didn't speak about serious matters because everybody was scared to death of being wire-tapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they wanted to set up contact with him rather than other officers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They, especially Ceca and Kameni, liked him and socialised with him as long as it was possible, before he was indicted, that is. They had a good relationship with him. I don't think that they socialised because of Ovcara. They just socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when -- why did they stop?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because of prison. Mr. Sljivancanin was here and they were also arrested. Some were convicted, some were quitted. Kameni was first convicted to 20 years and that was raised to five. Kinez got 20 years. I don't remember what happened to Ceca. The older man from my platoon, I showed him in that picture, he also got 20 year, Soskic. It was all for Ovcara. Maybe they socialise now. Now both Kameni and Sljivancanin are free men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why you had this coded system wherein you would ring three times and only then would he answer? Why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ceca knew that. Kameni did not have that number. Because they were looking for Mr. Sljivancanin. It's not only our services that were after him. There were also foreign services after him. We were especially afraid of manhunts and bounty hunters. Everything exists in the Balkans, and ultimately he was arrested. He was in hiding basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was all before he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not long before, because things were already under way then. There were arrests and wartime -- war crimes prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the OTP asked you to be a witness in the Sljivancanin case and you refused.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was preparing for some other case, perhaps Seselj, I'm not sure, when I was contacted by the Prosecutor working on Sljivancanin case. I refused, and I already explained. I told you that they had ways to make me testify. The Trial Chamber could issue a summons, but they didn't do that. They didn't ask the Trial Chamber to issue a binding order. And, anyway, I did not refuse impolitely. I just said that if I had a choice, I would not like to take part in that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you testified before this Tribunal in a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you must note that it was always in public. I insisted on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's true. Why were you reluctant to testify in the Sljivancanin case, in particular, unlike all the other cases where you did testify?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit personal, but I have more respect for that man than for all the others. I believe that he, too, is a casualty of what happened. That's my opinion. Although he was found guilty by this Court, but it's my right to still have my opinion. He is more humane, a better human being, although I don't know him that closely. We are not friends. It's just my personal opinion about him as a person. I told you, if they really wanted to have me testify, you know they had ways. A Judge issues a binding order and then I would have had to appear or they would have put me in prison for several months for contempt of court. Although, in his case, I would have chosen that over testifying against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you would have rather been convicted for contempt of court than testifying against Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would still have testified against all the others. And I would always testify in public session. Except -- except in the case of rape victims, everybody should testify in public, even insiders because in the end we'll all be judged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the proposal to testify in Sljivancanin as the Prosecution attempt to convict him and have you help them convict him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that was not my thinking. I just did not want to be a part of it. I did not want to be a part of anything that had to do with him. I did not want my name linked or mentioned anywhere in the Judgement. Although, as I say, they have ways. They had ways to make me testify. But I simply see that man differently. Although I did not get to know him very well, but I did see him on the front line. Or perhaps I was influenced by being friends with Kameni, or his being friends with Kameni. In any case, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But didn't it occur to you that by testifying in that case, considering that you have a high opinion of Veselin Sljivancanin, you would have helped his Defence, and you would have perhaps assisted the Court in getting a better understanding of him as a person and the events that occurred there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they did not contact me. From what I understand, both parties are able to contact witnesses; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say the Defence team did not contact you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you, as a witness, you could have said a lot of good things about him even as a Prosecution witness because the Prosecution was not forcing you to say anything against Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They do not impose anything to you. They listen to what you have to say. There is no coaching, no instruction, just as with the Defence teams. But I just did not want to appear in that trial as Prosecution witness. I probably would have been reluctant to appear as a Defence witness too. I just didn't want my name in that Judgement. And this changing of hats is also not me. It's -- the best thing, I believe, is to be neutral. And I did not consider myself as an expert or an important witness who would have -- who would have been able to help him or prove his guilt. I may have said something -- some things in my evidence in a confused way because that's how I lived them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in the Vukovar trial in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You mean when Kameni was the accused? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you called as a witness there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, by that time I had left Serbia. It's no secret that I was in the witness and victims unit in the relocation programme. Maybe I was difficult to reach. Maybe they were not able to find me. I testified in Belgrade twice but that had nothing to do with the SBWS. It had to do with Kosovo and with the Trnovo incident in Sarajevo. I testified without any protection measures. We did not have a system of protection measures anyway, at that time. Once I testified from here by videolink but it all concerned the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps testify in the Lovas case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Lovas before the war. People who live in Sid in that part of the Krajina know that there was a shop there where the boss was a man called Dule, and on very good terms we bought household appliances there on loan, and during the war I went only once. We came by car to the entrance to Lovas and went to back. I did not go to Lovas during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see on page 1 of your statement towards the bottom. It's the second page in English. You say that Milan Lancuzanin on that occasion when you met up at the railway station in Ruma, the conversation started when he said that Ovcara will be prosecuted in Serbia and that General Vasiljevic was set up at a trial in The Hague to blame that crime on the Territorial Defence of Vukovar and a certain number of volunteers from Leva Supoderica only to prove Sljivancanin's non-involvement in that crime.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not my words. I was just trying to convey what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you make this a bit clearer. How did you understand what Kameni said on that occasion, that General Vasiljevic was put up to it at -- at the trial in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know who General Vasiljevic is. He was the chief of the counter-intelligence service, and many of those involved in the war react to every mention of him with distaste and even revulsion. Don't ask me why. I watched his testimony in the Milosevic trial. I really wanted to see it, so I watched on the Internet. You know, there are conspiracy theories everywhere. I don't have a particular opinion. It could have been the way he described it. Perhaps not. I'm just saying what Kameni told us. All of us there are absolutely convinced that Sljivancanin is not guilty for what happened there. And despite his conviction, I have the right to think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not questioning your opinion. It's just that from your own words here, it follows that Vasiljevic was put up at the trial in The Hague to blame this crime on the TO Vukovar and the volunteers for the single purpose of proving Sljivancanin's non-involvement in Ovcara. When you say somebody was put up to do something, that implies that the person did not testify truthfully but gave false evidence in order to blame some things on one group of people rather than others.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is - my opinion was - that Serbia and Yugoslavia were prepared to do anything to prove that they were not involved, or their members were not involved. And to prove, instead, that the Territorial Defence and others were guilty, in fact. I believe that is so. And Vasiljevic is the spy master. A spy remains a spy. But that's how I remember Kameni's words at that meeting. To me, it also sounded like a conspiracy theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further below, you say that he even said - we're still talking about Kameni - that the trial in Serbia will follow that theory. This is some kind of forecast how the trial in the Ovcara case in Serbia will proceed. Did you follow that trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the media. Yes, I followed the reporting because many people I knew were involved. And what is said about the line the trial would take, it's -- it means that marginal people would be convicted, perpetrators, as if nobody in the top echelons knew anything. And that's why Kameni was afraid, because he considered himself a low-level participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then he says: "Namely, if it is proven, which I personally don't doubt would happen, that the crime was committed by members of the TO and the volunteers without the knowledge of the JNA, that will deflect all blame from Sljivancanin. He said that it was the purpose of the Serbian state to have anonymous people convicted of that crime rather than officials and officers because if the so-called Vukovar three, Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin, are convicted or characterised as involved in any way, then the state of Serbia would have to recognise its involvement in its -- in that conflict and that would mean paying a huge damages to the Republic of Croatia. As he explained, our grandchildren will be born indebted to the state of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he was saying that, did you have the impression that he received that information from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He seemed to have some knowledge. Otherwise, how would he have been able to talk like this? Perhaps I did not use his exact words when I described it because I didn't have a Dictaphone with me, but I tried to the best of my ability to convey what he said. The gist is there. And to me it all seemed very personal, very heart-felt, all this talk about war damages. And, now, in fact, we have a tribunal like that in this international tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the following sentence to me, the one in brackets: "During my conversations with the inspectors in charge of the Ovcara case, I got the impression that they know in detail what and how this crime happened. I realised this from the questions they were asking me. Then they correctly described people I knew and their role in it all, and they had other crimes in Bosnia for some of these individuals. Since they could not establish this after so many years, they therefore must have collected the information immediately following the crime and put it all aside." Is this your comment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After trial in Belgrade, and I still had not seen a single ICTY investigator, a judge accorded me one month of protection, but it so happened that they didn't have a police unit capable of doing that, so some police officers investigating war crimes were assigned to me. They took me to a hotel, and that's where they spoke to me like this. This is my account of what they were saying. They know all names, they know all details, some of which I didn't know. And this is my conclusion from that conversation with these police officers whose task it was to protect me, and eventually they brought me to The Hague on a plane. They were also interested in Ovcara and Djordje Soskic. They even knew when I went to see Soskic in Krusevac after the war. They knew even that. That's why I wrote these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page in English, I see that all three put forward suggestions as to what the story should be like if they come under investigation of either the Serbian judiciary or the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal. You go on to say that Kinez emphasised that it would be best if they told the truth but that Ceca did not agree. Ceca said, Kinez, the truth is what we now agree it is, and Ceca insisted on avoiding at all costs any involvement of the JNA by emphatically saying that they only saw uniforms of the Vukovar TO there."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Ceca was saying. Although a JNA uniform didn't mean a thing. TO members also wore the same uniforms. Volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that in accordance with what Kameni had said before, that any responsibility of JNA members should be avoided so that there should be no negative consequences for Serbia as regards war damages?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kameni didn't like that scenario, that he is convicted and that Serbia needn't pay anything after that. But he was convinced it would happen that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now what was the difference between what Kinez had said that, you should all say the truth, and Ceca's position that by no means anyone should speak about the JNA's involvement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither Ceca nor Kinez put forward their truth in my presence because, after all, I don't even know what that truth is. Ceca said a number of times, Well, we needn't involve Stoparic. He wasn't there with us. I even thought of leaving, but it would have been silly. None of them ever said that they killed anyone, this time included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this thesis about the uniforms of TO Vukovar was accepted by all three of them. Do you happen to know if they repeated that in the trial?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. When I went to Mr. Seselj's trial, once he mentioned that trial. But the transcripts and all that is something I cannot access. Maybe it can be found on some public site, but I never looked for it. I do believe that Kameni took this line of defence that he had indicated then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, you say what the conclusion was, what they had -- what they agreed on. Now you're saying that they were at a meeting in the staff or headquarters of the SRS and that Miroljub called them to return to Vukovar urgently. That they arrived in the afternoon, as you say here, that they sought out Miroljub and found him at Ovcara, that Kameni tried to take one of the prisoners out but Miroljub didn't allow it. When the killing began, Kameni gave the order to immediately get out of there - I mean the members of your unit - and that Miroljub tried to prevent him, and that this was what they had agreed on that they should say in case they were interrogated. Based on what we read here, what, in fact, is not true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events at Ovcara, what Miroljub told Kameni, and the rescue of that neighbour, I have no way of knowing if that's true. It is true that they came from Belgrade and that I spoke to them over the radio or the phone, and that they came in, in the evening. Everything else, apart from these facts, are things I don't know. These are mostly Kameni's words. Kameni said that everybody should say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, there is a statement of reasons, and you mark them with asterisks, and the second asterisk -- at the second asterisk, you say that this is a -- this is why they came up with this story. They say they only found members of the TO at Ovcara, in fact, they emphasised this: "This was Ceca's idea and it was composed into the story." It was put into the story.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ceca insisted on this. I can only make assumptions as to his reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that this was Ceca's idea, to me it sounds like it doesn't really reflect what in fact happened there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're looking at the these photographs, we also saw Ceca. I recognised him. He was wearing a JNA uniform. That may be one of his reasons. I can only make assumptions. Look at the photograph. You will see that he was wearing a new camouflage JNA uniform. Not everybody had such uniforms at the time. Yes, he was the one who insisted that this should be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the next bullet point or asterisk. "Talking about how men were removed from vehicles, they agreed that if anyone should ask what type of vehicle they were, they would say tractors and tractor-trailers without mentioning JNA vehicles."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's also what they agreed to say.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that had to do with the JNA was Ceca's idea. I don't know why he insisted on this JNA so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You may know - at least to the extent you followed the Vukovar trial - there was much insistence on tractors and tractor-trailers.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly followed through the media and the media didn't really cover all the details, so at the trial they were mentioning tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is merely because you said that you followed the Ovcara trial in Belgrade and probably the Ovcara here in this -- before this Tribunal, that it was nearly always said that the victims were taken away on tractor-trailers. You may have noticed that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I had limited means of following the trial in Belgrade, and I'm not sure when I wrote this, when exactly I wrote this. Possibly the -- the trial had already begun. Or maybe the investigation was under way. I can't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. I have finished examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have finished with my cross-examination.
